name: DNA Percentage Calculator
seoDesc: The DNA percentage of a genome is the share of its bases that code for protein. Free dna percentage calculator: enter your values and get coding percentage, n
summary:
The DNA percentage of a genome is the share of its bases that code for protein. It returns coding percentage, non-coding share, gene density and bases per gene, and the panel shows all of them at once.

Give the genome size and either the coding bases or a gene count with a mean gene length, and the page returns the coding percentage, the non-coding share, the gene density in genes per megabase and the mean bases per gene — the numbers that decide whether a genome is compact or mostly intergenic. Press Calculate and the results appear in the grey boxes; after the first press they keep up with every edit, so there is no page to reload. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the DNA Percentage
sections.html:
coding % = coding bases ÷ genome size × 100; gene density = genes ÷ genome size (Mb); bases per gene = genome (bp) ÷ genes

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
genomehaploid genome sizeMb
codingtotal length of coding sequenceMb
genesnumber of protein-coding genes—
gene densityhow tightly genes are packedgenes/Mb

sections.title: How do I use the DNA Percentage?
sections.html:
Every input sits in the same order the formula is written, so the page reads like the equation.

  1. Enter the genome size in megabases — one copy, not the diploid total.
  2. Enter the coding bases: the sum of all coding exons, which is what a genome annotation gives you as the total CDS length.
  3. Add the gene count if you want gene density and bases per gene; leave it as it is to skip those two lines.
  4. Compare the coding percentage across organisms: it is the single clearest number for how much of a genome is doing something.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: genome size of 3,000 Mb, coding bases of 90 Mb, gene count of 20,000.

Substituting them into the formula gives coding percentage of 3%, non-coding share of 97%, gene density of 6.67 genes/Mb, bases per gene of 150,000 bp, coding bases per gene of 4,500 bp.

Those numbers come from the same solver the page runs in your browser, not from an illustration, so typing different inputs moves the answer exactly as the arithmetic says.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
The number on its own is not a judgement. These are the bands most often used when the result is quoted in a paper, a report or a label:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
above 70 %Compactbacterial and archaeal genomes, and viral genomes
30 – 70 %Densesmall eukaryotes such as yeast and some fungi
10 – 30 %Typical eukaryoteinvertebrates and many plants
1 – 10 %Sparsevertebrates, including the human 1.5 %
below 1 %Very sparselarge plant and amphibian genomes dominated by repeats

  • The human figure is about 1.5 % coding and roughly 39 % in introns; the rest is intergenic sequence, much of it repetitive. A genome can be 50× larger than another with barely more genes — the difference is mostly repeats.

  • Coding percentage is not the same as exon percentage: exons include untranslated regions, so exon totals run higher than coding sequence totals.

  • Gene density and mean gene length move in opposite directions across taxa: compact genomes have short genes packed closely, which is why the bases-per-gene figure is worth reading next to the density.

  • Genome size here is haploid. A diploid cell contains twice this, which matters if you are converting to mass of DNA per cell.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
These are the errors that account for almost every wrong answer people bring to this calculator:

  • Using the diploid genome size and then comparing with published haploid percentages.
  • Entering the number of exons instead of the coding length.
  • Comparing coding percentages between an annotation that counts only reviewed genes and one that includes predicted open reading frames.
  • Assuming non-coding means non-functional: promoters, enhancers and non-coding RNA all live in the non-coding share.

sections.title: Calculators that go with this one
sections.html:
This tool answers one step of the question. The neighbouring steps have their own pages:

Coding capacity of DNA. Genome copy number. DNA concentration. GC content.

faq.q: What percentage of the human genome is coding?
faq.a: About 1.5 % — roughly 30 Mb of coding sequence in a 3 000 Mb haploid genome. Adding untranslated regions brings the exonic total to a few percent, and introns take about 39 %.

faq.q: Why do some genomes have almost no non-coding DNA?
faq.a: Because selection against carrying extra DNA is strong in fast-growing cells with large population sizes, which is the usual explanation for bacterial genome compaction.

faq.q: Is coding percentage the same as gene density?
faq.a: No. Gene density counts genes per megabase and says how packed the genes are; coding percentage measures how much of the sequence is coding. A genome can be gene-dense and still have a low coding percentage if its genes are mostly introns.

faq.q: Can I use this for a single gene or contig?
faq.a: Yes, with small numbers: a 2 000 bp gene with 1 500 bp of coding sequence is 75 % coding. The same formula works at any scale.

faq.q: What does the DNA Percentage actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns coding percentage, non-coding share, gene density and bases per gene. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.
